title: Multi-Table Joins
description: Trace optional relationship chains, complete composite keys and independent child aggregates without losing employees or multiplying workshop measures.

questions.question_text: What is a multi-table join?
options: A join limited to exactly two tables
A query chaining three or more tables together, each pair connected by its own join condition
A join that requires no conditions at all
A synonym for UNION of multiple tables
questions.explanation: A multi-table query combines several table expressions. Not every relationship must be a simple pairwise equality; the chosen join types and predicates must implement the required grain.

questions.question_text: Can different join types (INNER, LEFT, etc.) be mixed within one multi-table join chain?
options: No, every join in a chain must be the same type
Yes — each join's type is evaluated independently for what it preserves or drops at that step
Mixing join types always causes an error
Only the first join's type matters; the rest are ignored
questions.explanation: Mixed join types are legal, but preservation must be evaluated across the full logical chain; later required matches can remove earlier NULL extension.

questions.question_text: What risk grows as more tables are chained together in a join?
options: No additional risk — more tables is always safer
A single wrong or missing join condition anywhere in the chain can silently produce an accidental Cartesian-Product-style row explosion
The query automatically becomes read-only
SQL limits joins to at most 3 tables
questions.explanation: More join conditions mean more opportunities for one of them to be wrong, with the same silent-failure risk as a two-table join.

questions.question_text: Does the written order of JOIN clauses guarantee the actual execution order?
options: Yes, always executed exactly as written
No — the query optimizer may choose a different execution order for performance while preserving the same logical result
Execution order is random
Only the last JOIN clause is actually executed
questions.explanation: Optimizers frequently reorder joins internally; this is covered further in Chapter 35.

questions.question_text: What technique can improve readability of a very long, complex multi-table join?
options: Removing all WHERE clauses
Breaking it into named CTEs or views for intermediate steps
Always using CROSS JOIN instead of INNER JOIN
Combining every table into one via UNION first
questions.explanation: CTEs and views can decompose complex joins into more readable, named intermediate steps.

questions.question_text: In a chain of employees JOIN departments JOIN companies, what determines what data is available for the final SELECT?
options: Only the first table's columns
The combined columns from all successfully joined tables, subject to each join's matching conditions
Only the last table's columns
SQL automatically picks one representative table
questions.explanation: A multi-table join's final result draws from all tables in the chain, per their join conditions.

questions.question_text: Is it meaningful to have a LEFT JOIN followed by an INNER JOIN later in the same chain?
options: No, this combination is illegal
Yes — but care is needed, since a later INNER JOIN can effectively cancel out an earlier LEFT JOIN's NULL-preserving rows if it filters on a NULL-producing column
This always produces identical results to two LEFT JOINs
SQL automatically converts the later INNER JOIN into a LEFT JOIN
questions.explanation: An INNER JOIN later in the chain can require non-NULL values from an earlier LEFT JOIN's preserved rows, effectively undoing the outer preservation for those rows — a subtle multi-join interaction worth understanding.

questions.question_text: Why does adding several relationship links create more opportunities for predicate mistakes in a longer join chain?
options: Adding links makes every omitted key component harmless
There are more conditions overall, so more opportunities for any single one to be wrong and silently corrupt the whole result
Multi-table joins don't actually use join conditions
Join conditions only matter for the very last table in the chain
questions.explanation: Every relationship predicate matters. More joins add opportunities for an incorrect path or multiplicity assumption, not a mathematical rule that one predicate becomes intrinsically more important.

questions.question_text: What should be fixed before adding a third relation?
options: The required output identity and grain
Only alias length
Only table creation order
Only physical file size
questions.explanation: Every added relationship must preserve the intended result contract.

questions.question_text: What can a later inner join through an optional department do?
options: Automatically preserve every employee
Remove employees whose chain has no matching company
Turn every key into NULL
Create a company for each employee
questions.explanation: NULL-extension at one step can be rejected by a later required match.

questions.question_text: What guarantees at most one department match here?
options: The word JOIN alone
The complete department key relationship
A repeated display name
ORDER BY alone
questions.explanation: Cardinality depends on constraints and complete predicates.

questions.question_text: Why include tenant_id in a scoped composite relationship?
options: It always speeds every query
It replaces authentication
The local number alone can match another tenant’s entity
It makes all NULLs equal
questions.explanation: All required key components must identify the intended relationship.

questions.question_text: Two instructors and three registrations join independently. How many matching pairs can result?
options: Two
Three
Five
Six
questions.explanation: The independent child populations multiply.

questions.question_text: Why is SUM DISTINCT fee not a general multiplication repair?
options: Different registrations can legitimately have equal fees
It always includes every identity
It creates missing workshops
It enforces foreign keys
questions.explanation: Deduplicating numeric values is not deduplicating business facts.

questions.question_text: What grain should each independent aggregate branch expose?
options: Every raw child row
At most one row per required workshop identity
One global unqualified total always
One row per display label only
questions.explanation: Preaggregation prevents independent branch multiplication.

questions.question_text: When is EXISTS useful instead of appending detail pairs?
options: When every child column must be returned
When result order is automatic
When only qualifying evidence is required
When all joins are forbidden
questions.explanation: A predicate can preserve outer identity without one row per witness.

questions.question_text: Can two separate EXISTS clauses use different child witnesses?
options: No, they always identify one shared row
Only without indexes
Only if both are empty
Yes
questions.explanation: Same-row requirements must be expressed deliberately.

questions.question_text: Does written join order always fix physical execution order?
options: No
Yes, for every engine
Only for three tables
Only when aliases are short
questions.explanation: Eligible transformations preserve semantics within outer-join constraints.

questions.question_text: What fixture challenges optional chains?
options: Only fully connected rows
Missing first match and missing later match cases
Only one company
Only unique display names
questions.explanation: Complete happy paths cannot expose preservation defects.

questions.question_text: What should be investigated before adding final DISTINCT?
options: Only font size
Only result column labels
The first unexpected cardinality change and its relationship predicate
Only line count
questions.explanation: DISTINCT can hide legitimate pairs or a faulty intermediate grain.

coding_problems.title: Retain employees through an optional company chain
coding_problems.task: Return employee_id, department, company for every employee. Department and company are optional. Order by employee_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE companies(company_id INT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(40)); CREATE TABLE departments(department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(40),company_id INT NULL); CREATE TABLE employees(employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,department_id INT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO companies VALUES(1,'North Labs'); INSERT INTO departments VALUES(10,'Engineering',1),(20,'Field',NULL); INSERT INTO employees VALUES(1,10),(2,20),(3,NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT e.employee_id,d.name AS department,c.name AS company FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id=e.department_id LEFT JOIN companies c ON c.company_id=d.company_id ORDER BY e.employee_id;
coding_problems.expected:
employee_id	department	company
1	Engineering	North Labs
2	Field	NULL
3	NULL	NULL
coding_problems.explanation: Two left joins retain each employee while unique dimension keys prevent multiplication.

coding_problems.title: Aggregate independent workshop branches safely
coding_problems.task: Return workshop_id, instructor_count, paid_total for every workshop. Count workshop_instructors rows and sum only confirmed payment amounts. Missing child groups give zero. Order by workshop_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE workshops(workshop_id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE workshop_instructors(instructor_link_id INT PRIMARY KEY,workshop_id INT); CREATE TABLE workshop_payments(payment_id INT PRIMARY KEY,workshop_id INT,amount INT NOT NULL,status VARCHAR(12));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO workshops VALUES(1),(2); INSERT INTO workshop_instructors VALUES(1,1),(2,1); INSERT INTO workshop_payments VALUES(1,1,10,'confirmed'),(2,1,10,'confirmed'),(3,1,10,'confirmed'),(4,1,100,'cancelled');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT w.workshop_id,COALESCE(i.instructor_count,0) AS instructor_count,COALESCE(p.paid_total,0) AS paid_total FROM workshops w LEFT JOIN (SELECT workshop_id,COUNT(*) AS instructor_count FROM workshop_instructors GROUP BY workshop_id) i ON i.workshop_id=w.workshop_id LEFT JOIN (SELECT workshop_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_total FROM workshop_payments WHERE status='confirmed' GROUP BY workshop_id) p ON p.workshop_id=w.workshop_id ORDER BY w.workshop_id;
hints: Group each child table before joining.
Count identities and sum every eligible payment.
coding_problems.explanation: Each child summary has one row per workshop, so the two branches do not cross-multiply.

notes:
## Name the result grain before connecting another table

A multi-table join combines several table expressions through explicit relationships. The useful question is not merely how to add a third JOIN, but which real-world identity each final row should represent. An employee-directory row, a course enrollment and a company summary are different grains. Each additional relationship can preserve, remove or multiply the existing population depending on join type, predicate and cardinality.

Imagine a directory linking employees to departments and departments to companies. The required result is one row per employee with optional department and company labels. The employee identifier is the output identity. Department and company primary keys provide at-most-one matches at each step. Without those key assumptions, a short syntactically valid chain can produce several rows per employee and violate the report contract.

## Draw the relationship path explicitly

Assume departments has department_id as its key and a nullable company_id reference. Employees has employee_id as its key and a nullable department_id reference. Companies has company_id as its key. The relationship path is employee to department to company. A condition connecting an employee directly to an unrelated company identifier would be a different rule, not an equivalent shortcut because both columns happen to contain integers.

```sql
SELECT e.employee_id,e.name AS employee_name,
       d.name AS department,c.name AS company
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id=e.department_id
LEFT JOIN companies c ON c.company_id=d.company_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
```

With Asha in Engineering at North Labs, Jon in a department with no company, and Mira with no department, the report retains all three employees. Asha has both labels, Jon has a department and NULL company, and Mira has NULL for both optional labels. The second LEFT JOIN keeps the optional chain optional. The query does not invent employees for an unreferenced company or an empty department.

## Evaluate preservation across the complete chain

Replacing the second LEFT JOIN with an INNER JOIN requiring d.company_id=c.company_id can remove Jon and Mira. Their intermediate NULLs cannot satisfy ordinary equality to a company key. The first left join did preserve them at its logical step, but a later required match removed them. This is a common reason an apparently optional relationship becomes mandatory in the final result.

A WHERE condition on an optional company's attribute can have the same effect if it rejects NULL-extended rows. Put a condition in ON when it defines which company information qualifies while the employee must remain. Put it in WHERE when the report truly requires only employees associated with a qualifying company. The correct placement follows the desired population, not a blanket rule that every filter belongs in one clause.

## Verify every key component and alias

A tenant-scoped department may be identified by tenant_id and department_number together. Joining only department_number can connect an employee to another tenant's same-numbered department. Include every required key component and trusted scope condition. A matching display name or a numeric value that happens to be unique in one fixture does not establish the intended relationship across all allowed data.

Aliases should make ownership of each identifier visible. In a longer chain, several tables can have an id, status or name column. Qualify those references and choose unambiguous output aliases. A query that accidentally binds an unqualified name to the wrong scope can return plausible results on uniform sample values. Give connected tables different labels in the fixture so a wrong reference becomes observable.

## Predict one-to-many multiplication

Suppose one workshop has two instructors and three registrations. Joining both independent child populations directly to the workshop can produce six instructor-registration pairs. Summing a registration fee over that joined result counts each registration once per instructor. The multiplication is a consequence of the relationship graph, not an arithmetic failure inside SUM.

| Workshop children | Instructor rows | Registration rows | Combined pairs |
|---|---|---|---|
| One workshop | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| No instructors under inner join | 0 | 3 | 0 |
| One instructor | 1 | 3 | 3 |

If the report requires one row per workshop with instructor_count and paid_total, aggregate each independent child population to workshop grain before joining. Alternatively, use separately scoped correlated aggregates when appropriate. DISTINCT on the fee is not a general repair: two separate registrations can legitimately pay the same amount and both must contribute. Preserve business identities rather than deduplicating values that only look repeated.

## Preaggregate independent measures at their owner

```sql
SELECT w.workshop_id,
       COALESCE(i.instructor_count,0) AS instructor_count,
       COALESCE(p.paid_total,0) AS paid_total
FROM workshops w
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT workshop_id,COUNT(*) AS instructor_count
  FROM workshop_instructors GROUP BY workshop_id
) i ON i.workshop_id=w.workshop_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT workshop_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_total
  FROM workshop_payments WHERE status='confirmed'
  GROUP BY workshop_id
) p ON p.workshop_id=w.workshop_id
ORDER BY w.workshop_id;
```

Each derived relation has at most one row per workshop under its GROUP BY. The joins therefore preserve workshop grain without cross-multiplying the independent details. COALESCE supplies the stated zero policy for missing child groups. If amounts are nullable or unknown must remain distinct from zero, the aggregate and fallback policy need revision. The example assumes known payment amounts and a report where no eligible payments means zero.

## Keep existence questions separate from detail joins

If the report only asks which employees have at least one approved training enrollment, an EXISTS predicate can retain each outer employee without appending every enrollment pair. A chain joining courses and approvals can be appropriate when their detail columns are required, but it can multiply rows when they are used merely as evidence. Choose the logical operation from the desired output rather than adding joins reflexively.

Multiple eligibility conditions may need to be satisfied by the same related row. Two separate EXISTS predicates can find different witnesses, while one combined predicate requires one witness satisfying both. A multi-table join can make that relationship explicit if all predicates connect the correct identities. Test counterexamples where each condition is satisfied by a different child so an accidental weakening does not pass unnoticed.

## Separate logical join order from physical execution

The written query defines a logical result and dependencies. The optimizer can reorder eligible inner joins and transform derived expressions while preserving semantics. Outer joins have preservation constraints that restrict valid transformations. It is inaccurate to claim either that the engine always executes joins exactly left to right or that every outer-join order can be freely exchanged.

Use EXPLAIN to inspect the actual selected plan and an appropriate controlled execution measurement when performance matters. Indexes on relationship keys can help, but row estimates, distribution, filter selectivity and intermediate multiplicity also influence cost. A large accidental intermediate product can dominate work even when each individual equality lookup has an index. Correct cardinality is both a semantic and a tuning concern.

## Build a fixture that challenges the whole path

Include an employee with a complete chain, one with a missing first relationship, one with a department lacking a company, and two employees sharing a display name. Include unused departments and companies so the preserved population is tested. For aggregate reports, include several children on each independent branch, equal-valued payments, a workshop with no children and a cancelled payment that must not contribute.

Inspect intermediate grains during debugging without changing the required final result. Count identities at each step and identify the first point where legitimate rows disappear or unexpected pairs appear. A final DISTINCT can conceal that evidence. Keep the minimal failing fixture and predicate explanation so a future query extension can rerun the same preservation and multiplication checks.

Keep schema constraints beside the fixture. A claimed one-to-one lookup supported only by today's data can become one-to-many after a valid insert. The final result should depend on declared relationship semantics, not on an unstated accidental uniqueness assumption in a small sample.

## Solve two relationship-chain exercises

First exercise: return every employee with optional department and company labels. The solution uses the complete employee-department-company path with two left joins and stable employee ordering. Change the final join to INNER in a separate experiment and predict which optional cases disappear. Explain why that changed result answers a stricter population question rather than an equivalent optimization.

Second exercise: return every workshop with independent instructor count and confirmed-payment total. Preaggregate both branches before joining and verify that two instructors plus three ten-unit payments produce count two and total thirty, not count six or total sixty. Continue with [join cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality), [LEFT JOIN](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/left-join) and [aggregate query optimization](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/aggregate-query-optimization) to preserve grain while extending a query.
